basics.name: Deyan Dobrinov
basics.label: Team lead at Dext
basics.summary: I am a software developer with more than 14 years of professional experience. In the past several years I am mostly working on Ruby/Rails web projects. I believe that every complex problem has a simple solution, which could be found if you understand where the complexity comes from. I enjoy doing that. I like good UX, and I fight for it.

headline: I find the simple solution hiding inside complex systems.

facts.label: shipping software since 2007, at SAP, Funding Circle and Dext, where I now report to the CTO.
I love great UI and UX, and I fight for it: in specs, in code review, down to the last pixel.
Dext's payments system, built from the first commit: supplier and payroll runs, strong customer authentication.
shipped in 2026 with coding agents; 5 of them in Rust, in one month.

engineering.name: Making complex systems simple
engineering.proof: Search rebuilt on Elasticsearch · a monolith split into a service
engineering.detail: At Dext, replaced an over-complex PostgreSQL search with Elasticsearch, so the app became a thin layer around a search engine. Extracted manual data extraction from the monolith into its own service through incremental releases.

engineering.name: Fighting for great UX
engineering.proof: Dext's main app rebuilt in React · [Symtrail](https://apps.apple.com/app/symtrail/id6782177088), an iOS app in 20 languages · Wunderkind, Shape and Circle
engineering.detail: Good UX rarely survives a deadline on its own, so I argue for it: when we plan, when we review, and on the final screen. I design and build the interfaces of my own products, Wunderkind, Symtrail, Shape and Circle, and send back anything that's off by a pixel. One in twenty of my prompts is a screenshot with one line about what is wrong.

engineering.name: Shipping risky change safely
engineering.proof: Front-end rewrite with no incremental release, team of 8
engineering.detail: Moved Dext’s main app to React + TypeScript on a new GraphQL API and rolled it out with a low amount of risk.

engineering.name: Payments and financial data
engineering.proof: Built Dext's payments service · OCR tables, bank statements, invoices · P2P lending
engineering.detail: Table extraction from OCR data, transaction and line-item flows and PDF splitting at Dext. Technical-debt work at Funding Circle, a peer-to-peer lending platform.

engineering.name: Leading and mentoring
engineering.proof: Teams of up to 8 · can mentor 14 technologies
engineering.detail: Team lead for 2 engineers and 1 QA, then development lead reporting to the CTO. Can mentor in Ruby, Rails, TypeScript, React, GraphQL, PostgreSQL and 8 more.

ai.name: At work, I review every line agents write
ai.proof: At Dext, no agent-written change merges until I have read the diff line by line
ai.detail: Agents draft; I review. I open the branch in a diff viewer, comment on specific lines and hand the comments back until the change is one I would have written myself. Side projects can move fast; production code at work does not skip this step.

aiPractice.owned: Every line that merges at work
verifiedBy: Line-by-line review in a diff viewer

ai.name: Products AI agents can operate safely
ai.proof: Approval gates, read-only modes and untrusted-input handling in Investor, Trace and Circle
ai.detail: Agents read freely but every write waits for the person. Secrets stay on the machine: Circle drives Chromium over a private pipe instead of the open debugging port, and Trace strips visitor text before an agent reads it.

ai.name: Hard software with coding agents
ai.proof: Schema and Shape: 54k lines of Rust in a month, signed releases on 3 operating systems
ai.detail: Hand-written SQL and Rails parsers, a layered graph layout with routed edges, and a three-way merge so diagrams live in git. Both ship skills that let other agents use them.

ai.name: Reviving hand-built code with AI
ai.proof: Wunderkind: Elo engine written by hand in 2025, grown with agents and live in 2026
ai.detail: The core I wrote by hand set the rules; agents built the question bank, duels, leagues and parent reports around it.

highlights.title: A front-end rewrite with no incremental release
highlights.hook: Led 8 people moving Dext’s main app to React, TypeScript and GraphQL, then shipped it in one go.
highlights.problem: Dext’s main application needed a new front-end stack, and a big part of it had to be rewritten. Incremental releases were not possible.
highlights.did: Led a team of 8. We rewrote a large part of the app in React + TypeScript on a newly created GraphQL API.
highlights.outcome: Rolled out with a low amount of risk.

highlights.title: Dext's payments system, from the first commit
highlights.hook: The most complex thing I have built: Dext customers pay suppliers and payroll from the bills Dext already reads.
highlights.problem: Dext read the bills its customers had to pay, but the paying happened somewhere else. Moving real money meant bank accounts, batch transfers and strong customer authentication on every payment.
highlights.did: I started the payments service in December 2024 and wrote about half of its 773 commits: accounts with a banking partner, batch payment runs to suppliers, strong customer authentication for every payment and withdrawal, fees, and webhooks that keep both sides in sync. In the main app I added payroll payment runs, payroll CSV import and reconciliation through Xero bank feeds.
highlights.outcome: In production in Dext: supplier and payroll payment runs, fees, withdrawals, and reconciliation through Xero bank feeds.

highlights.title: Wunderkind: an adaptive maths coach, by hand and then with agents
highlights.hook: Wrote the Elo engine by hand in 2025, then grew it into a live platform with agents in 2026.
highlights.problem: Practice only helps when the questions are neither too easy nor too hard for that child.
highlights.did: I wrote an Elo engine that aims each child at a 70% success rate, calibrates new students and widens its search when the bank runs short. After a nine-month pause I revived it with coding agents: an authored question bank up to grade 12, live duels with matchmaking, leagues and a weekly report to parents.
highlights.outcome: Live at wunderkind.bg with 728 tests. Output per commit grew from about 65 to about 367 lines after the revival.

projects.name: Trace
projects.description: Web analytics for the agentic era. An analyst agent turns how people use a site into improvement insights tied to its KPIs, each insight copies out as a prompt for a coding agent, and once the change ships Trace measures whether it worked. Written in Rust.

projects.name: Investor
projects.description: A local-first investment planner: double-entry books, scenario projections and tax reporting, with an MCP server so an AI assistant can read the books and record changes you approve. Everything stays in one encrypted .invest file. Rust compiled to WebAssembly, with a desktop app.

projects.name: Circle
projects.description: An open-source, Arc-style browser built in Rust on Chromium (CEF), with spaces, a command bar, split view and an MCP server for AI agents.

projects.name: Shape
projects.description: One board for a whole project: mindmaps, kanban boards, timelines, screen sketches and decisions, kept as a plain-text file in the repo. A board copies out as a Markdown spec for a coding agent to build from. Rust compiled to WebAssembly.

projects.name: Schema
projects.description: Interactive ER diagrams and visual git diffs for Postgres, MySQL, SQLite and Rails schemas, plus a design mode that turns sketched changes into a spec an agent implements. One Rust engine compiled to WebAssembly runs the CLI, the browser viewer and embeddable diagrams.

projects.name: Lurepedia
projects.description: A moderated community wiki for fishing lures, with a review queue for edits and look-alike detection for photos.

projects.name: Symtrail
projects.description: A private symptom diary for children on the App Store: offline, no account, 20 languages, and a PDF report for the paediatrician.

projects.name: Dzhambaz
projects.description: A Chrome extension that shows the real market price of a car on Bulgarian listing sites.

projects.name: Wunderkind

projects.description: JsonMe is a web application allowing software engineers to maintain a resume in json format and keep it in their Github/Gitlab profile. The CV that you are looking at the moment is generated with it.
projects.revival: Rebuilt as {me}: a static CV and blog that developers keep in their own repo and publish with a GitHub Action.

This was working well so I wrote a web application for this. More about the motivation behind the project could be found here - https://medium.com/@ddobrinov/text-based- stand-ups-de741fa6c724.

llms.source: 2,081 of my prompts to Claude Code, Sep–Oct 2026

patterns.name: Brain-dump the spec
patterns.how: When I start something new, I write everything I know in one long prompt: what it is for, who uses it, what it must and must not do.
patterns.achieves: The model starts from my intent instead of a generic version of the idea.

patterns.name: Pseudocode as the prompt
patterns.how: When I already know the logic, I write the signature, data shape or if/then steps and let the model fill in the code.
patterns.achieves: The code follows my design, not the one the model would have picked.

patterns.name: A concrete example
patterns.how: When a behaviour is ambiguous, I describe one real scenario step by step.
patterns.achieves: The model builds for the case that matters and I can check the result against it.

patterns.name: Add one more constraint
patterns.how: When an answer is close but not right, I resend the prompt with the one sentence that was missing.
patterns.achieves: A precise result without starting the conversation over.

patterns.name: Defer scope
patterns.how: I say what to leave for later ("for now", "skip", "we will extend later").
patterns.achieves: Small increments that ship, instead of one change that does everything.

patterns.name: Pick up where I left off
patterns.how: After an interruption I ask the model where we are and what is left.
patterns.achieves: I switch between projects without losing the thread.

patterns.name: Steer by naming code
patterns.how: I name the exact function, class or variable to rename, move or inline.
patterns.achieves: The structure and naming I want, without writing the change myself.

patterns.name: Cut it back
patterns.how: Once something works, I ask to inline single-use code, remove indirection and comments, or start over if it got too complex.
patterns.achieves: Code a person can read and maintain, not just code that passes.

patterns.name: Let the model decide
patterns.how: For choices that are cheap to change, I tell the model to decide and keep going.
patterns.achieves: My attention goes to the decisions that matter.

patterns.name: Use my own tools
patterns.how: I point the model at tools I built, like Schema and Shape, to visualise a database or a flow.
patterns.achieves: A picture of the system we both work from.

patterns.name: Ask why first
patterns.how: Before I accept a change, I ask why it is needed, where it is used and whether something simpler would do.
patterns.achieves: I understand every line I ship and catch code that should not exist.

patterns.name: Push back with an alternative
patterns.how: When I disagree, I say so and describe what I want instead.
patterns.achieves: Design decisions stay mine.

patterns.name: Review the diff myself
patterns.how: At work I always review what agents write: I open the branch in a diff viewer, comment on lines and hand the comments back to the model.
patterns.achieves: Nothing merges that I have not read.

patterns.name: Make it test itself
patterns.how: I make the model test its work in a real browser, or send role-played agents (engineers, a child, a CTO) to try it and critique it.
patterns.achieves: Bugs and product gaps found before I look.

patterns.name: Screenshot plus one line
patterns.how: For UI problems, I attach a screenshot and write one sentence about what is wrong.
patterns.achieves: Precise visual feedback in seconds.

patterns.name: Triage by number
patterns.how: When the model lists issues or options, I reply with the numbers to fix, skip or decide.
patterns.achieves: Quick decisions on many items at once.

patterns.name: Pass on outside feedback
patterns.how: I paste reviews from people and other tools and ask the model to act on them.
patterns.achieves: Feedback turns into changes the same day.

patterns.name: Explain it simply
patterns.how: When I meet unfamiliar code or an option I do not understand, I ask for a plain explanation with an example.
patterns.achieves: I learn the parts of the system I did not write.

patterns.name: Write prompts for other models
patterns.how: I ask one model to write the prompt for another tool or session.
patterns.achieves: Context moves between tools without me retyping it.

patterns.name: Git by one-liners
patterns.how: I hand git chores to the model in short commands: commit, squash, fold, cherry-pick, push.
patterns.achieves: A clean history without the busywork.

llms.gap: I rarely put every constraint in the first prompt or ask for a plan first: 48 prompts resend the previous one with one more sentence, and only about 15 ask for a plan before code.
